newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Court judgement bad for Seven - ARL.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Court judgement bad for Seven - ARL.

text.p: The Australian Federal Court's decision on Friday to uphold the News Ltd Super League appeal would create problems for the exclusive agreements Seven Network Ltd has to televise rugby union and Australian rules football, the Australian Rugby League (ARL) said.

"What the court has now demonstrated is that if the loyalty agreements are anti-competitive then Channel Seven has a big problem with its broadcasting rights over the Australian Rugby Union and the AFL," said Mark O'Brien, an ARL spokesman.

"From my quick understanding of what the court has done, they're saying the contracts to broadcast sport may be outlawed under the Trade Practices Act if given exclusively to one network," O'Brien told reporters outside the Federal court.
Earlier, the court had found in favour of News Ltd's appeal against an earlier court ruling which banned News' Super League rugby league competition before the year 2000.
The court found five year loyalty agreements signed by the ARL clubs and the ARL contravened the anti-monopoly rules in the Trade Practices act and News Ltd-aligned clubs could break them.
However, it also found that News Ltd had induced clubs to break their one-year agreements with the ARL for 1995 and ruled that News would have to pay damages for disruption to the ARL in 1995.
The court said damages would be decided at a later date.
The ARL later said it would consider an appeal to the decision and that there was likely to be two competitions next year.
The Seven Network has exclusive agreements to broadcast the major Australian Rugby Union matches and the Australian Football League's (AFL) national Australian rules competition.
It also on-sells these rights to pay television operators Foxtel and Optus Vision.
Seven shares ended one cent firmer at A$4.05.
